web_evidence.title: The Development of the Reimaginative and Reconstructive in Historiographic Metafiction: 1960-2007
web_evidence.note: The Ohio State dissertation describes Ragtime's voice as a backward-looking omniscient narrator that moves among characters and historical digressions; it treats occasional 'we' as the historian-like narrator's editorial usage.

web_evidence.title: “The Real-World Act:” The Attainment of First Personas in Doctorow’s Ragtime
web_evidence.note: The scholarly article says the Little Boy hypothesis is undermined by the novel's constant third-person narrative voice and concludes that the narrator operates outside the story as an all-seeing director.

web_evidence.title: E. L. Doctorow’s Ragtime in the Context of Historiographic Metafiction – A Study
web_evidence.note: The study repeatedly identifies an omniscient narrator and documents only one first-person-singular instance near the ending, while acknowledging debate over whether that voice can be associated with the Little Boy.

web_evidence.title: Ragtime: Key Facts
web_evidence.note: Explicitly classifies the novel as third-person omniscient and notes that the anonymous, ambiguous narrator only occasionally uses first-person plural.

web_evidence.title: Ragtime

person_note: The quote set repeatedly exhibits the novel's controlling omniscient, reportorial third-person narration across characters, historical figures, private thoughts, and broad social history. The main complication is q02116: web research identifies it as the narrator's sole first-person-singular appearance near the ending, not ordinary dialogue, and some critics infer that the narrator is the grown Little Boy. Likewise, editorial forms such as 'our history' can suggest a collective American voice. These moments make the narrator's identity deliberately ambiguous, but they do not form sustained first-person chapters or an autonomous first-person strand. Under the methodology's controlling-person rule, the isolated ending sentence and editorial national plurals do not warrant FIRST or ALTERNATING; the base narration remains THIRD. The remaining uncertainty concerns who the omniscient voice may represent, not the predominant narrative person.
